## 2.1.1.1.1 GPQA Diamond (no tools)

**GPQA Diamond (no tools)** is an evaluation that
measures graduate-level scientific reasoning using the open-access [GPQA benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) [[4](/gpt-6-2-astra-sol/references#ref-ref09 "David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland, Jackson Petty, Richard Yuanzhe Pang, Julien Dirani, et al. “ GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark .” Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022 .")].

The Diamond subset contains 198 questions in biology, chemistry, and
physics. For each question, the model selects one of four answers
without using external tools. We report the percentage of questions
answered correctly.

GPT-6.2 Astra answered 97 percent of questions correctly. GPT-6.2 Sol
and GPT-6 Astra each answered 96 percent correctly. Both GPT-6.2 models
exceeded our indicative threshold of 83 percent, which we based on the
performance of earlier models assessed as meeting the High threshold
using a broader suite that included ProtocolQA Open-Ended, Tacit
Knowledge & Troubleshooting, and TroubleshootingBench.

## 2.1.1.1.2 Multi-select Virology Troubleshooting

**Multi-select Virology Troubleshooting** is an
evaluation that uses [SecureBio](https://securebio.org/)’s
Virology Capabilities Test [[5](/gpt-6-2-astra-sol/references#ref-ref10 "Jasper Götting, Pedro Medeiros, Jon G Sanders, Nathaniel Li, Long Phan, Karam Elabd, et al. “ Virology Capabilities Test (VCT): A Multimodal Virology Q&A Benchmark .” Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16137 .")] to measure whether models can identify
correct explanations or next steps in laboratory troubleshooting
scenarios.

Virologists wrote and peer-reviewed the 322 questions. Each question
presents a laboratory scenario, sometimes with an image, and four to ten
statements. The model earns credit only if it selects every true
statement and leaves every false statement unselected. We report the
share of questions answered correctly on a single attempt (pass@1). The
refusal-adjusted score also gives credit when the model declines or
withholds the requested assistance for policy reasons.

The SecureBio pre-print reports that after recruiting 36 virology
experts, the mean accuracy on the Virology Capabilities Test was 22.1
percent, and the 78th-percentile score was 30.8 percent. We therefore
use 31 percent as our indicative threshold, approximating the
80th-percentile expert score.

GPT-6.2 Astra answered 61.80 percent of questions correctly on a
single attempt, compared with 55.40 percent for GPT-6.2 Sol and 55.78
percent for GPT-6 Astra. Both GPT-6.2 models exceeded the indicative
threshold. On the refusal-adjusted measure, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 61.93
percent and GPT-6.2 Sol scored 55.71 percent, compared with 63.11
percent for GPT-6 Astra.

## 3.4.1 HealthBench Professional

**HealthBench Professional** [[17](/gpt-6-2-astra-sol/references#ref-ref33 "Rebecca Soskin Hicks, Mikhail Trofimov, Dominick Lim, Rahul K. Arora, Foivos Tsimpourlas, Preston Bowman, et al. “ HealthBench Professional: Evaluating Large Language Models on Real Clinician Chats .” Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27470 .")] is an [open-access
OpenAI benchmark](https://cdn.openai.com/dd128428-0184-4e25-b155-3a7686c7d744/HealthBench-Professional.pdf) of assistance with difficult clinical tasks,
developed in collaboration with clinicians. We report it in place of the
original [HealthBench](https://openai.com/index/healthbench/)
[[18](/gpt-6-2-astra-sol/references#ref-ref34 "Rahul K. Arora, Jason Wei, Rebecca Soskin Hicks, Preston Bowman, Joaquin Quiñonero-Candela, Foivos Tsimpourlas, et al. “ HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health .” Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775 .")], which has become less
informative for recent models, as we’ve reported in recent system
cards.

Because raw rubric scores can reward longer responses, we report both
raw scores and scores adjusted for response length. On the 0–100 scale,
responses receive a 1.47-point penalty per 500 characters above 2,000
and a corresponding bonus below 2,000; models are not told the
adjustment in their prompts. The [benchmark
paper](https://cdn.openai.com/dd128428-0184-4e25-b155-3a7686c7d744/HealthBench-Professional.pdf) [[17](/gpt-6-2-astra-sol/references#ref-ref33 "Rebecca Soskin Hicks, Mikhail Trofimov, Dominick Lim, Rahul K. Arora, Foivos Tsimpourlas, Preston Bowman, et al. “ HealthBench Professional: Evaluating Large Language Models on Real Clinician Chats .” Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27470 .")] describes
the method.

Both launch models scored higher than GPT-6 Astra after adjusting for
response length and lower on raw rubric scores, reflecting shorter
responses. GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol scored 66.3 and 65.9 after
adjustment, compared with 64.7 for GPT-6 Astra. Their raw scores were
66.0 and 65.5 versus 68.2, and their responses averaged 1,884 and 1,869
characters versus 3,185.

system_card_raw_sections.MentalHealthBench: ## 3.4.3 MentalHealthBench [**MentalHealthBench**](https://cdn.openai.com/ctf-cdn/MentalHealthBench_A_Comprehensive_Benchmark_of_AI_Capabilities_in_Realistic_Mental_Health_Conversations.pdf) [[19](/gpt-6-2-astra-sol/references#ref-ref35 "Ali Malik, Declan Grabb, Rebecca Soskin Hicks, Rahul K. Arora, Preston Bowman, Michael Sharman, et al. “ MentalHealthBench: An Expert-Informed Benchmark of AI Capabilities in Realistic Mental Health Conversations .” Available at: https://cdn.openai.com/ctf-cdn/MentalHealthBench_A_Comprehensive_Benchmark_of_AI_Capabilities_in_Realistic_Mental_Health_Conversations.pdf .")] is an open benchmark developed with mental health experts for measuring how AI systems respond in realistic mental health conversations. It consists of 1,215 synthetic conversations covering diverse scenarios ranging from daily well-being topics to urgent mental health emergencies. Each conversation task is paired with clinician-authored rubric criteria that can be used to score a new model response. We include more details about the evaluation design in the paper. Each response receives a rubric-based score clipped to 0–100 percent. We average four independent responses within each task, then average task scores. Standard errors are computed across task means: 1,215 overall, 650 non-acute, 221 high-acuity, and 344 emergent tasks. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol scored 53.3 percent and 50.9 percent on MentalHealthBench, versus 58.7 percent for GPT‑6 Astra and 57.9 percent for GPT-6.1 Sol. Both scored lower at each acuity level. ‘Context seeking and assessment’, or asking for more context to provide more helpful answers, accounted for about half of each model’s overall decline, substantially larger than other behavioral axes of MentalHealthBench like providing actionable guidance or harm avoidance and refusals. We observe that reductions in context seeking behavior are broader than mental health conversations and may be related to GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol’s increased preference for concise and actionable responses. ### Figure 26 ![Figure 26.
